newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - MCI stays cautious on future.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - MCI stays cautious on future.

text.p: MCI Communications Corp said core long-distance revenues in the first quarter grew at twice the pace of its key long distance rivals, but cautioned that minute and revenue growth could moderate in coming quarters.

In an interview, MCI Chief Financial Officer Doug Maine downplayed the effect any softness might have on MCI, saying the trend was concentrated in residential markets the company has retreated from in favor of focusing on higher-margin customers.
Maine said and that it planned to maintain its focus on long-term strategies, not short-term growth measures.
MCI's strategy of replacing discount-seeking residential callers with customers willing to pay for value-added services should insulate it from the industry-wide downdraft, he said.

The MCI executive reiterated that his company's proposed merger with British Telecommunications Plc buys it time to gear up for a broad national entry into the U.S. market for local phone services as opportunities develop.
"The strategy is to abandon the low end of the market for now until (MCI is able to offer) local service nationally as part of a bundled package of services," Maine said.
"The fact that we are merging with British Telecom means our stock essentially trades as a multiple of BT's, giving us a greater window to execute our strategy," he said.
The two stocks essentially have traded in tandem since the merger deal was announced in early November.
Maine made the comments after the release of MCI's first quarter earnings, which at $0.42 a share were flat versus the year-ago quarter and in line with Wall Street expectations.
For several quarters, MCI has asked Wall Street to measure its performance according to the progress it makes in moving ahead on long-term strategies not near-term financial results.
In response, financial analysts' expectations have flattened, with the First Call estimate consensus ranging from $0.42 to $0.43 per share in each of 1997's four quarters.

Bear Stearns analyst Bette Massick said MCI appeared to be making progress in cleaning up its customer base by reducing the number of "spinners," or customers who switch to which ever provider offers the cheapest calling plan.

"They are clearly focusing on what will follow the merger," Massick said Thurday, adding that unless she learns something new, she planned to leave her earnings estimate for the 1997 year at $1.65 per share.

MCI's caution toward the residential long-distance market echoes concerns by rival AT&T Corp, which described competitive pressures and a variety of profit-taxing customer retention techniques in its own first quarter report Monday.

Until remaining barriers to entering the local services market drop, Maine said his company will forgo chasing low-end consumers using AT&T's practice of writing checks to customers as a tactic for making them switch providers.
Maine repeated MCI's reluctance to use marketing dollars to chase the consumers in the current market environment.

He said the company's strategy to attack the residential market, as in business markets, hinges on plans to offer a bundle of integrated services, including long distance, voice messaging, Internet access along with local phone access.
"That way we (will) get twice the revenes for the same marketing costs," Maine said of the strategy to integrate local services with a broader set of service offerings.

If favorable, the new rules on local access charges expected to be announced May 8 by the U.S. Federal Communications Commission could lead the company to move more aggressively into local services market, he said.
MCI was off 1 at 37-3/4 in mid-afternoon trading. British Telecom shares in London closed down seven pence at 450-3/4.
-- Eric Auchard, New York newsdesk, 212-859-1736
